There are certain limitations on the environment in which a microprocessor system can be stored and operated. Operating the system in a proper environment will help prevent future repairs.
1. System should not be stored or operated in a dusty enviroment.
2. The system should only be operated within the manufacturers specified temperature limitations.
3. The system should always be plugged into a grounded outlet.
4. The system must not be operated near an unshielded power supply of other equipment. Strong emissions from power supplies can force crystals to vibrate at the wrong frequency.
5. The system should always be turned off before attaching or detaching hardware from the system.
Different precautions must be taken when handling various components of the microprocessor circuits.
However, you cannot treat CMOS ICS the same way. Handling CMOS ICS may destroy them by static discharges from the body.
Dropping it may crack the chip, destroying it. The ICs legs can also be bent so when inserted into the PC board the legs do not line up with the board or socket.
There are two types of ICs used in the 68000 microprocessor system: CMOS and TTL. CMOS stands for Complimentary Metal Oxide Semiconductor and TTL stands for Transistor-Transistor Logic.

These are two of the most common technologies used in the construction of ICs. TTL chips can work at a higher speed but have high power consumption. The CMOS is slower but uses less power than TTL. CMOS is very susceptible to static electricity.

Placing an IC into a circuit requires special attention and sometimes special equipment.

Soldering an IC, especially a CMOS chip, can destroy the device no matter how careful you are. Because of this, most ICs are now inserted into sockets. The sockets are soldered to the PC board before the IC is inserted.
Before trying to insert an IC, you should check that its legs are straight and evenly spaced.
On a IC, pin 1 is identified by a dot or notch located on the upper surface of the IC. Pin numbers run sequentially from the dot or notch in a counterclockwise direction.
Inserting a chip backwards can destroy the chip. To insert the IC, line up all its legs with the socket connectors then press it down gently.

Use a chip extractor to remove an IC. When this tool is not available use a small flat tip screwdriver, carefully prying at either end of the chip until it can be removed in a straight upward fashion.
There are IC insertion and removal tools available that make insertion and removal simple.
Thus far, we have discussed troubleshooting and corrective maintenance.

As the name implies, this maintenance is accomplished before the system has a chance to fail. For example, suppose that your microprocessor is operating correctly, there are no signs of system failure.
However, you decide to measure the output voltages of the power supply once a month. One month you find the measurements show that the usual +5V to each chip is now measuring +8V.
Even though the system operates correctly, the output voltage may eventually damage some of the chips in the microprocessor system.
To eliminate this possible problem you decide to adjust the power supply. This process is known as preventative maintenance.
When a printed circuit board becomes coated by a layer of dust, the particles act as an insulator and traps heat close to the components.
Preventative maintenance is performed on a regular time schedule before something breaks.

A computer repair technician must select tools to use which are appropriate to the troubleshooting task.
DISCUSSION
Often you will choose tools that you are familiar with. However, knowing how to use other tools can speed up the troubleshooting process.
In your studies of electronics, you have learned that multimeters and oscilloscopes are valuable in determining correct circuit operation and for troubleshooting faulted circuits.
In each area of electronics, different types of test equipment provide the best means for circuit measurements. Digital or microprocessor electronics are not exceptions.

In DC circuits, the multimeter is the best choice for measuring circuit values of voltage, current and resistance. In AC circuits, the oscilloscope is most valuable for determining the characteristics of various waveforms.
In digital electronics, the oscilloscope and multimeter are used, along with several other types of test instruments. In this course, the multimeter, oscilloscope and logic probe have been used.
Other types of test equipment are available. The testing of digital circuitry is different from analog circuitry in several ways.

Digital circuits use low DC voltages; 0, 5 and 12 VDC are most common. Digital circuits normally do not have AC voltages present. Digital circuits do not require resistance checks due to the design of the ICs.
Digital circuits often rely on timing. Since ICs can not be repaired, measuring input and output signals is the troubleshooting method used.

Because of these differences, several special types of digital test instruments have been developed. Before discussing the specialized test instruments let's first examine the multimeter and the oscilloscope.
The multimeter is the most commonly used test instrument in DC and AC circuits. However, it is not the most commonly used test instrument in digital circuits.
Multimeters measure DC and AC voltage, DC and AC current and resistances. Some even test transistors, diodes and capacitors.
In digital electronics, multimeters are used primarily to measure operating power, that is Vcc, and check for open or shorted wires on PC cards. Vcc is normally a DC voltage between 5 and 12 volts.
The trend in digital electronics is to use the lowest Vcc values that the chips can run on. Many circuits today are being designed to run on 1 volt, which represents a high condition.
PC card wires are checked by measuring continuity between points on the card. Continuity indicates a good connection, no continuity indicates an open wire.

The logic highs and lows may also be measured using a multimeter. A high is normally between 2 and 12 VDC and a low is between 0 and 2 VDC. Remember, you must have knowledge about the IC technology you are troubleshooting.
Many have different ranges of values that represent high and low conditions. As long as the logic levels are constant, a multimeter will give an accurate reading of HIGH or LOW.

If the levels are changing (pulse inputs and outputs) the multimeter is of little use. Since there are other means to measure operating voltages and logic levels, the multimeter is not used very often, only for continuity checks.
The oscilloscope is a lot more expensive than the multimeter, however, there are not many electronic shops that do not have at least one.
OSCILLOSCOPE
HORIZONTAL
VERTICALAL
The oscilloscope gives a visual display of a voltage waveform and measures AC and DC voltages, periods and phase. In digital circuits, the oscilloscope is one of the most versatile instruments.

The oscilloscope can detect abnormalities in waveforms that other instruments cannot detect. Characteristics such as amplitude, rise and fall times, pulse width, period and frequency can be quickly determined from oscilloscope measurements.
An oscilloscope can also be used to measure the logic highs and lows which are DC values. In addition, pulse and square waves can be measured.
One of the big advantages of using a dual trace oscilloscope is that two waveforms can be measured at the same time. In this way, time relationships can be analyzed.

However, the oscilloscope has one disadvantage when used in microprocessor systems. Only one or two waveforms can usually be displayed at one time. This disadvantage is overcome by using an oscilloscope multiplexer.

The multiplexer allows up to 16 signals to be viewed on the oscilloscope at the same time. If you were trying to check the output of the data bus, you can see where being able to look at all the lines can be important.
The logic probe is the least expensive of all digital test instruments. It is especially designed to be used with digital circuits.
This is due to the inherent inability of the human eye to see changes in the LEDs at high clock rates.

Consider the common incandescent light bulb in a home or office. When the light is switched on, a voltage is applied to the bulb at a 60 Hz rate. The bulb is actually turning on and off 60 times a second; too fast for the human eye to recognize.
Logic probes only measure logic levels, not DC voltage levels. The probe provides a simple means of measuring highs, lows and pulses.

The probe is nothing more than one or more LED indicators that illuminate for certain types of signals. A logic probe can indicate a high signal, a low signal, single pulse, multiple pulses or an open or bad level.
Although logic probes can be useful when troubleshooting digital circuits, they are most effective when troubleshooting individual logic gates at slow clock speeds.
The logic analyzer is basically a special type of multichannel oscilloscope that has the ability to display logic levels, pulse trains of highs and lows, in several formats.
PROBE THRESHOLD LEVEL
LOGIC ANALYZER
Logic analyzers are expensive and only used in complex digital circuits. One type of format is the TIMING DIAGRAM. Several pulse waveforms are displayed in the correct time relationship.
Dual channel oscilloscopes, in most cases, can only display two waveforms. The second type of format is the BIT or BIT PATTERN.
The sequence of 1s and 0s from a functional circuit can be compared to the pattern of a faulty circuit to detect errors. Oscilloscopes and logic probes cannot do this.
Another type of format that may be included on some logic analyzers is the CODED format. The coded format changes the ones and zeros to either octal or hexadecimal code.

The code for a particular point in a circuit can then be compared to a given code in a technical manual or to the code present in a functional circuit. Any differences between the measured code and the reference code indicates a fault.
The signature analyzer is somewhat like the logic analyzer without the waveform display. It uses the coded format by measuring pulse trains of highs and lows.
PROBE TEST
UNSTABLE
SIGNATURE

HEWLETT PACKARD
Signature analyzers are used to locate faults to the component level in microprocessor based systems. The instrument converts a series of ones and zeros at a given test point to a hexadecimal code.
The code is called the signature for that particular test point. Then, by comparing the signature to the known signature, you can identify faults.
Again, the signature analyzer is only used in very complex circuits where the cost of the instrument can be justified.

The current tracer and logic pulser are very simple test instruments that measure pulsating current at a particular point in a circuit. Their appearance is very similar to the logic probe depending on the manufacturer.
LOGIC PULSER
CURRENT TRACER
SENSITIVITY
The current tracer and logic pulser are used to find points in a digital circuit that are stuck, that is, the point remains at a logic 1 or 0 all the time.
It is particularly difficult to isolate a bad IC component when several components are connected together. The current tracer and logic pulser make the job easier.

The logic pulser is used to inject a pulsating signal into the circuit if normal signal levels remain at a high, low or floating state. The current tracer is used to trace the current paths through the circuit.
An LED on the current tracer illuminates when the signal at a particular point is pulsating. No LED indication indicates a fault and by signal tracing, the bad component can be located.
The logic clip is also a very simple tool used to determine logic levels on an IC. The clip attaches to an IC where it makes contact with each pin.

On the logic clip are LEDs or lamps or just pins, one for each pin connection to the IC. The LED or lamp illuminates brightly for a high and is off for a low. A pulsing signal is identified by either a dimly illuminated LED or one that is rapidly blinking.
Even though test instruments provide vital information on the operation of a microprocessor, there are other tools a technician can use to make their job easier.
Visual inspections must be performed carefully before, during, and after troubleshooting. Visual inspections identify mechanical damage, heat damage, misuse, etc.
Before you even test a circuit using the test instruments, you should look for damaged components. A burnt resistor is a sure sign of a problem, and not necessarily a bad resistor!
After troubleshooting and repair you should do another visual inspection to ensure that the repair process did not cause any damage to the system.

Diagnostic routines are programs used in the microprocessor to test out the system. These programs are normally supplied by the system manufacturer. If not, and you know how to program a microprocessor, your own diagnostic routines can be written.
The only disadvantage of diagnostic programs is that the microprocessor system must operate well enough to load and execute a program.
The advantage of diagnostic routines is time saving. Most diagnostic programs will, at a minimum, identify what section is faulted.
Some diagnostic routines even identify which component is faulted! No troubleshooting is required.
